Chapter 14 — Growth Modification: Class II, Open/Deep Bite & Multidimensional Problems

Plain text is your original summary, kept word-for-word. Coloured boxes are genuine 7th-edition additions (green = new, amber = changed/corrected); red marks important cautions. Figures sit in the right margin (zoom to read the book caption).
Class II Growth Modification
  • Patients with a Class II growth pattern have some combination of deficient forward mandibular growth and excessive maxillary growth that is more likely to be downward than forward.

I Perspectives on Growth Modification

  • Fig. 14.2 is a hypothetical plot of the response to functional appliance treatment, illustrating the difference between absolute stimulation (larger as an adult) and temporal stimulation (acceleration of growth). Fig 14.2
  • Some published data suggest that timing mandibular growth modification to coincide with the mandibular growth spurt can provide growth change beyond what usually occurs.
Updated stance (7th) Using cervical vertebral maturation (CVM) to time growth modification is now described as a method with "supporters, detractors, and questionable validity" — the 6th edition called it only a method with "supporters and detractors."

II Functional Appliances

  • By definition, a functional appliance is one that changes the posture of the mandible and causes the patient to hold it open and/or forward for Class II correction or back or open for Class III correction.
  • Even if contact with the teeth is minimized, soft tissue elasticity can create a restraining force on forward growth of the maxilla, so that a "headgear effect" is observed "in most functional appliance" Fig 14.4.
  • The monobloc is generally considered the forerunner of all functional appliances, but the activator was the first functional appliance to be widely accepted.
  • In 1960, the most popular were the Bionator Fig 14.5 and the Frankel appliance Fig 14.6.
  • With functional appliances, additional growth is supposed to occur in response to the movement of the mandibular condyle out of the fossa, mediated by reduced pressure on the condylar tissues or by altered muscle tension on the condyle. What does happen with treatment for patients with Class II relationships is:
    • A modest change in the size of the mandible's overall length averaged 0.16 mm per month (range, 0.09 to 0.24 mm per month)
    • Often a reorientation of the maxilla and the mandible, usually facilitated by a clockwise tipping of the occlusal plane Fig 14.8 and a rotation of the maxilla, the mandible, or both.
    • A reduction in forward growth of the maxilla also occurs (the "headgear effect"). This is typically less than 1 mm per year.
  • Although the Twin-Block appliance is reputed to be quite successful in stimulating mandibular growth in preadolescents, published data show that it is equally successful at the peak of the growth spurt as when used early, and the changes it produces are a combination of skeletal (40%) and dental (60%).
New in 7th ed — evidence A meta-analysis of short-term Twin-Block treatment showed the classic combination of Class II changes — proclination of lower incisors, retroclination of upper incisors, with the molar/overjet correction — and there was limited, if any, headgear effect.
New in 7th ed — evidence A long-term meta-analysis of removable functional appliances found that on average they produced about 1.5 mm of mandibular change compared with controls, with the range up to 3.4 mm — the Twin-Block being the second-best performer.
  • Functional appliances also can influence eruption of posterior and anterior teeth. If upper posterior teeth are prohibited from erupting and moving forward while lower posterior teeth are erupting up and forward, the resulting rotation of the occlusal plane and forward movement of the dentition will contribute to correction of the Class II dental relationship. (It is important to keep in mind that eruption of posterior teeth in a mandibular-deficient patient is beneficial only when good vertical growth is occurring) Fig 14.9

III Headgear

  • Restraint of mandibular growth along with restraint of maxillary growth is never observed. Fig 14.10
  • Headgear force against the maxillary molar teeth often tips them distally, often accompanied by some distal movement of the maxillary premolars as force is transmitted to them by the supercrestal gingival fibers.
  • There also is a vertical effect on the posterior teeth, extrusive with cervical headgear, "possibly" intrusive with high-pull headgear (true intrusion rarely occurs, but downward movement of the maxilla and posterior teeth is impeded)

IV Functional Appliances Vs Headgear: Some Clarity From Randomized Clinical Trials

  • The data from all the trials show that on average, children treated with either headgear or a functional appliance had a small but statistically significant improvement in their jaw relationship during the treatment period (late preadolescence and early adolescence), whereas the untreated children did not.
  • There is no question now that growth modification in children with Class II problems is effective—it works in the majority of the patients.
  • Did early treatment with headgear or a functional appliance produce a long-term difference when early treatment outcomes are compared with the outcome of later (adolescent) treatment? It appears that:
    • Skeletal changes are likely to be produced by early treatment with headgear or a functional appliance but tend to be diminished or eliminated by subsequent growth and later treatment.
    • Early treatment does not reduce the number of children who require extractions during a second phase of treatment or the number who eventually require orthognathic surgery.
    • The duration of phase 2 treatment is quite similar in those with and without a first phase of early treatment aimed at growth modification.
  • It seems clear that for most children with Class II problems, early treatment is no more effective than later treatment, and it is more efficient to modify growth during the adolescent growth spurt than before adolescence.
  • If early treatment is pursued, when the maxillary skeletal and dental effects that go along with any enhancement of mandibular growth are considered, functional appliances usually are preferred.
  • For many patients who do not have a definitive maxillary excess or mandibular deficiency as part of the Class II problem, either a functional appliance or headgear can be used.
  • Headgear probably is a better choice for a patient with frank maxillary excess.
New in 7th ed — evidence In the clinical trials, children who had early treatment had fewer incidents of incisor trauma, especially with functional appliances.
New in 7th ed — evidence No link to obstructive sleep apnea: two newer studies and a 2019 AAO White Paper failed to find any connection between headgear wear or extractions and obstructive sleep apnea.

V Fixed Class II Correctors

Herbst Appliance

  • Generate both skeletal and dental changes.
  • Herbst appliance now is recommended for the early permanent dentition when the changes are more localized to the protrusion of the mandible but not for use in the mixed dentition (because of substantial rebound in the immediate posttreatment period).
  • Because Herbst appliance can produce maxillary posterior dental intrusion, it provides better results when used in patients with normal or slightly long anterior face height.
  • Although less patient compliance is an advantage, breakage has long been recognized as a significant disadvantage.

MARA Appliance

  • A more durable and less bulky alternative to the Herbst appliance
  • The MARA appears to have a significant if temporary headgear effect.
  • It affects the mandible less than the Twin-Block and Herbst appliances.
  • The combination of maxillary dental retraction and mandibular dental protrusion that all functional appliances (fixed and removable) create is similar to the effect of interarch elastics. This "Class II elastics effect" can be quite helpful in children who have maxillary dental protrusion and mandibular dental retrusion in conjunction with a Class II skeletal problem (mandibular dental protrusion usually contraindicates functional appliance treatment).
  • At present the effects of fixed functional appliances on the temporomandibular joint are poorly documented but do not appear to differ from the low prevalence of temporomandibular dysfunction problems in removable functionals.
  • It appears that the Forsus device produces more vertical skeletal and dental changes and the Twin-Block device provides more positive mandibular changes. Others making this comparison have found not only the different mandibular effects, but also more maxillary restriction and mandibular incisor proclination with the Forsus appliance.
  • MARA appliance has more maxillary restriction but less mandibular advancement effect than the Twin-Block.
New in 7th ed — numbers Quantified effect of fixed functional appliances: about 1° of SNA reduction per year, 1° of SNB increase per year, and <2° of ANB change per year.
Updated number (7th) Adding skeletal anchorage to a fixed functional appliance has only small skeletal effects (SNB <1°, ANB ~1°) — a revision of the 6th edition's statement that supplemental anchorage "does not affect the skeletal changes."
New in 7th ed — evidence Head-to-head, there is little difference in overjet reduction or other cephalometric changes between the various fixed correctors, with little patient-centered-outcome evidence to separate them.

VI Components of Removable and Fixed Class II Functional Appliances

Components to Advance the Mandible

  • Components to advance the mandible are often classified as active or passive. (it is different than dental active or passive component)
  • If the patient has to voluntarily move the mandible to avoid an interference, the appliance is active. If it allows only a restricted path of movement or closure, it is passive.
  • By that definition, appliances such as the activator, Bionator, Twin-Block, and MARA are active appliances, and the Herbst and Forsus are passive appliances.
  • Flanges, either against the mandibular alveolar mucosa below the mandibular molars "in activator and bionator" or lingual pads "in FR-II" contacting the tissue behind the lower incisors, provide the stimulus to posture the mandible to a new more anterior position Fig 14.15.
  • All the fixed appliances have the advantage of full-time wear. The disadvantage is that pressure against the teeth, which produces compensatory incisor and molar movements, cannot be avoided.

Vertical Control Components

  • When acrylic or wire is placed in contact with a tooth and the vertical dimension is opened past the normal postural position, the stretch of the soft tissues will exert an intrusive force on the teeth Fig 14.16.
  • Intrusion usually does not occur, probably because the force is not constant, but eruption is likely to be impeded.
  • Vertical control of this type is usually included in the design of any functional appliance.
  • Lingual shields prevent the resting tongue from being placed between the teeth Fig 14.17. This has the effect of enhancing tooth eruption. A lingual shield is particularly important if eruption of posterior teeth is desired on one side but not the other. One caution here is that this component often limits the patient's acceptance of the appliance because speaking can be difficult.

Stabilizing, Passive & Active Components

  • Stabilizing: Clasps often help the first-time wearer adapt to the appliance. The labial bow across the maxillary incisor teeth should be considered as a stabilizing component Fig 14.18.
  • Passive: Plastic buccal shields and lip pads, both of which are incorporated into the Frankel appliance Fig 14.19. Their disadvantage is that they add to the potential for soft tissue irritation that can inhibit patient compliance. The addition of a vertical stop over the lower incisors decreases irritation from the lip pads (because it stabilizes the appliance).
  • Active Expansion and Alignment: Modified activators added the elements of active plates to an activator framework so that teeth could be moved while jaw growth was being manipulated (such as jackscrew and midline split, wire springs to reposition the incisors). Incorporating active elements into a functional removable appliance has three problems:
    1. The more tooth movement, the less skeletal change can be used or achieved
    2. Precise tooth positions cannot be achieved with springs or screws in removable appliances.
    3. The tooth movement will be only from tipping, which is less stable and more susceptible to relapse.

Treatment Procedures — Pretreatment Alignment

  • The patient's ability to posture the mandible forward at least 4 to 6 mm is critical. Some patients incisor interferences prevent the mandible from being advanced to the correct position for the bite registration.
  • The problem can be either lingual displacement of the upper incisors (a Class II division 2 incisor pattern) or irregular and crowded incisors in either arch. (It must be kept in mind that facial displacement of the lower incisors, which would be produced by aligning them without creating space to do so, contraindicates functional appliance treatment that would move them even further facially.)
  • Either fixed or removable functional appliances can be used for this purpose.
  • To control the tendency of the repositioned incisors to relapse lingually, they should be held in place for several months after being repositioned.

Impressions and Working Bite

  • "Working bite" (register the desired mandibular position) (same for fixed and removable appliances)
  • If buccal shields or lip pads are to be used, it is important not to overextend the impressions so that tissue is displaced because this makes it difficult or impossible to accurately locate the appliance components in the vestibule.
  • Unless an asymmetry is to be corrected, the mandible should be advanced symmetrically so that the pretreatment midline relationships do not change appreciably.
  • 4 to 6 mm mandibular advancement and a 3 to 4 mm (minimum) vertical opening, but always one that is comfortable for the patient and does not move the incisors past an edge-to-edge incisor relationship.
  • It appears that quite large, modest, or relatively small advancements all can produce growth modification and that there is little difference in the results.
  • If eruption of upper and lower posterior teeth is to be limited, as in a child with excessive vertical face height, the working bite should be taken with the patient open 2 to 3 mm past the resting vertical dimension (i.e., 5 to 6 mm total opening in the molar region) so that the soft tissue stretch against the bite blocks will produce a continuous force opposing eruption.

VII Clinical Management of Functional Appliances

Removable Functional Appliances

  • With any functional appliance, a break-in period is helpful. Having the child wear the appliance only a short time per day to begin with and increasing this time gradually over the first few weeks.
  • Problems with speech are greatest when there is a bulk of acrylic behind or between the anterior teeth.
  • It is known now that skeletal growth has a circadian rhythm. Most growth occurs during the evening hours when growth hormone is being secreted; active eruption of teeth occurs during the same time period, typically between 8 pm and midnight or 1 am. (To take practical advantage of this time period, it is suggested that children wear functional appliances from after the evening meal until they awaken in the morning, which should be approximately 12 hours per day).
  • A good appointment schedule is to recall the child at 1 and 2 weeks after insertion for inspection of the tissues and the appliance. (If a sore spot develops, the child should be encouraged to wear the appliance a few hours each day for 2 days before the appointment so that the source of the problem can be determined accurately).
  • Because the initial mandibular advancement is limited to a modest 4 to 6 mm and many children require more anteroposterior correction, a new appliance may be needed after 6 to 12 months of wear and a favorable response. It is a good idea to reevaluate progress at 8 to 10 months after delivery with new records or at least a progress cephalometric radiograph.

Fixed Functional Appliances

  • Accommodation increases rapidly after several days.
  • Soft tissue irritation is not a major problem with the Herbst, Twin-Block, or later versions of the Forsus, but the teeth may be more sensitive than with removable functional appliances.
  • Patients should be instructed that the appliance is meant to remind them to posture the mandible forward and not to force the mandible forward with heavy pressure on the teeth. (In this sense, sore teeth for an extended amount of time may indicate poor cooperation).
  • With the Herbst, after a positive treatment response is noted, changes in the pin and tube length can be made during treatment to increase the amount of advancement simply by adding sleeves to the pin.
  • With the MARA, advancement is achieved with shims on the elbow wire to advance it.
  • A fixed (or removable) Twin-Block appliance can have plastic resin added to the inclines to increase the advancement without totally remaking the appliance.
  • It is possible to make a Twin-Block appliance partially fixed and partially removable. This also is possible with a Herbst appliance.
  • With Forsus appliance, it can be helpful to place lingual root torque in the incisors to combat proclination.
  • Forsus appliance can be reactivated (usually a reasonable activation is 2 mm) for more advancement by either placement of a split spacer on the pushrod, moving from the distal aspect of the canine to the distal aspect of the premolar for pushrod placement, or use of a new, longer pushrod Fig 14.30. Different length pushrods on the right and left sides can be used to correct mild asymmetry.
  • Fixed functional appliances usually are worn for 8 to 12 months.
  • For all the fixed functional appliances, adverse vertical effects (opening of the posterior bite) or adverse horizontal effects (Class III over-correction of Class II relapse) can occur. These can be countered with either a posterior box elastic or Class III or Class II elastics, respectively.
  • If the patient is still in the mixed dentition period when the desired correction is achieved, the Herbst appliance or MARA can be removed at that point, but it is important to consider use of a removable functional appliance of the activator or Bionator type as a retainer when this is done. This retainer should be worn approximately 12 hours per day until the patient is ready for the second phase of fixed appliance treatment. Avoiding a prolonged retention period is a major reason for delaying fixed functional treatment until the adolescent growth spurt is beginning.
7th-ed correction For Forsus, the 7th edition says to place buccal root torque in the incisors to combat proclination (the line above, from the 6th edition, reads "lingual root torque"). Buccal root torque is the biomechanically correct direction for uprighting proclined lower incisors.

Treatment Procedure With Headgear

  • Components of Headgear: two major components — the facebow and the neckstrap or headcap.
  • Effects of Extraoral Force on the Maxilla: The studies have shown that headgear force can decrease the amount of forward and/or downward growth of the maxilla by changing the pattern of apposition of bone at the sutures.
  • Class II correction is obtained as the mandible grows downward and forward normally while similar forward growth of the maxilla is restrained, so mandibular growth is a necessary part of the treatment response to headgear.
  • There is some evidence of increased mandibular growth during treatment with headgear; whatever the mechanism, headgear does appear to have both maxillary and mandibular effects.
  • In a growing patient, headgear must be worn regularly for at least 10 to 12 hours per day to be effective.
  • The current recommendation is a force of 12 to 16 ounces (350 to 450 gm) per side.
  • It is important to control the vertical position of the maxilla and the maxillary posterior teeth. Downward movement of either the maxilla or the maxillary posterior teeth tends to project mandibular growth more vertically, which nullifies most of the forward mandibular growth that reduces the Class II relationship Fig 14.34. For these reasons, high-pull headgear usually is preferred. Directing the line of force closer to the center of resistance is another major reason for including an upward direction of pull for most children who have headgear force to the maxilla.
  • Selection of Headgear Type (three major decisions to be made):
    • First, the headgear anchorage location must be chosen to provide a preferred vertical component (headcap or neckstrap). The more signs of a vertically excessive growth pattern, the higher the direction of pull and vice versa. Cervical headgear does not always aggravate vertical problems, especially when there is good vertical mandibular growth and minimal distal movement of maxillary molars, which is the best predictor of vertical opening.
    • Second, how the headgear is to be attached to the dentition. The usual arrangement is a facebow to the large headgear tubes on the permanent first molars. Alternatively, a removable maxillary splint or a functional appliance can be fitted to the maxillary teeth and the facebow attached to it. This may be indicated for children with excessive vertical growth.
    • Finally, a decision must be made as to whether bodily movement or tipping of the teeth is desired. The length and position of the outer headgear bow and the form of anchorage (headcap or neckstrap) determine the vector of force and its relationship to the center of resistance of the tooth. As in any growth modification treatment, tooth movement usually is an undesirable side effect, and with headgear, tooth movement is minimized because the teeth must move bodily if they move at all. The various combinations of force direction (anchorage), length of outer bow, and position of outer bow are diagrammatically illustrated in Fig 14.35.
New in 7th ed The improvement in mandibular growth and chin prominence during headgear treatment is now specified to occur when headgear is used with a posterior biteplate.
  • Clinical Management of Headgear: Bands, not bonded tubes, are necessary to accommodate the heavy forces.
  • As a Class II molar relationship is corrected, the relative forward movement of the lower arch will produce a crossbite tendency unless the upper arch width is expanded (the inner bow should be expanded by 2 mm symmetrically so that when it is placed in one tube, it rests just outside the other tube).
  • Fitting and adjustment of the preformed facebow, are shown in Figs 14.36 and 14.37.
  • A spring mechanism or tension module—not elastic bands or straps—is strongly recommended to provide the force. The springs deliver consistent forces that can be documented and easily adjusted.
  • The spring attachment is adjusted with the patient sitting up or standing, not reclining.
  • It is usually a good idea to start with a low force level to acclimate the patient to the headgear and then gradually increase the force.
  • Headgear is definitely not indicated during vigorous activity, bicycle riding, or general roughhousing.
  • The headgear straps must be equipped with a safety-release mechanism to prevent the bow from springing back at patient.
New figure detail (7th) The headgear force module is now dot-calibrated Fig 14.36 — 1, 2, 3, or 4 dots = 4, 8, 12, or 16 ounces of force, respectively — so the delivered force can be set and documented precisely.
Combined Vertical and Anteroposterior Problems
  • It can be difficult to determine the extent to which skeletal disproportions versus tooth eruption deviations are involved.
  • It is apparent that a patient with deficient vertical growth also would have deficient eruption of the teeth, and vice versa.

I Short Face / Deep Bite

Short-face problems are easier to manage with growth modification.

  • The reduced face height is often accompanied by everted and prominent lips that would be normal if the face height were normal.
  • Growth is expressed in an anterior direction, with a tendency toward upward and forward rotation of the mandible.
  • In a patient with Class II malocclusion, one way to correct such problems is with cervical headgear, taking advantage of the extrusive tendency of extraoral force.
  • The other way is to use a functional appliance (usually with mandibular advancement, depending on the anteroposterior jaw relationship) that inhibits eruption of maxillary posterior teeth and allows free eruption of the mandibular posterior teeth.
  • Rotation of the occlusal plane down in front makes it easier to achieve a Class I molar relationship. The desired rotation of the occlusal plane occurs when the lower molar erupts more than the upper, which means that, all other factors being equal, the functional appliance would be preferred.
  • The treatment of these short-face Class II patients is a balance between the anteroposterior and the vertical reactions to treatment. For this to be accomplished, all vertical eruption is blocked while an appliance with the mandible advanced is used, which will create a posterior open bite when the appliance is not in place. When the Class II jaw relationship is corrected, the posterior bite block gradually is cut away from the lower molars and premolars while correct overbite is maintained anteriorly, so that slow eruption of lower posterior teeth back into occlusion can occur.
  • Fixed functional appliances are not good choices in the treatment of short-face problems (with its propensity to intrude the upper molars).

II Long Face / Open Bite

  • Excessive growth of the "maxilla" in children with Class II malocclusion has more of a vertical than an anteroposterior component.
  • The goal of growth modification treatment for long-face problems is to maintain the vertical position of the maxilla and inhibit eruption of the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth Fig 14.41.
  • There are several possible approaches to doing this during preadolescent and adolescent growth:
    • High-Pull Headgear to the Maxillary First Molars — 14 hours a day, 12 ounces per side. This does not control eruption of the lower molars, which limits its effectiveness in some patients.
    • High-Pull Headgear to a Maxillary Splint — a more effective headgear approach for children with excessive vertical development. Splint can be extended forward to contact the incisors if desired. An appliance of this type would be most useful in a child with excessive vertical development of the entire maxillary arch and too much exposure of the maxillary incisors (a long-face child without anterior open bite). Unfortunately, the maxillary splint still allows mandibular posterior teeth to erupt.
    • Functional Appliance With Bite Blocks — a more effective alternative. The primary purpose of the appliance is to inhibit vertical descent of the maxilla and eruption of posterior teeth in both arches. The bite must be opened past the normal resting vertical dimension if molar eruption is to be affected, so the stretch of the soft tissues exerts a vertical intrusive force on the posterior teeth. Because there is no compensatory posterior eruption, all mandibular growth should be directed more anteriorly, at least to the extent that the overbite allows.
    • High-Pull Headgear to a Functional Appliance With Bite Blocks — the most aggressive approach to maxillary vertical excess and a Class II jaw relationship, which has been recommended as a way to treat the most severely affected long-face patients. In reality, the addition of headgear appears to provide little if any more vertical skeletal and dental control and has only a modest anteroposterior maxillary skeletal impact.
  • For severely affected children with the long-face pattern, the only successful treatment methods are intrusion of posterior teeth by means of skeletal anchorage and segmental maxillary osteotomy.
Facial Asymmetry in Children
  • An asymmetry problem involving only the maxilla is quite rare and almost always is due to trauma to that part of the face.
  • The mandible is involved in 85% to 90% of facial asymmetry cases because of a growth problem.
  • However, asymmetric mandibular growth has secondary effects on the maxilla, and both jaws are likely to become involved as the asymmetry develops.

I Asymmetric Mandibular Deficiency

(hemifacial microsomia and condylar fracture)

  • There are three aspects to the differential diagnosis between these two conditions:
    1. A congenital anomaly of any severity is likely to be noticed at birth, and the later the asymmetric deficiency arises, the more likely it is to be due to a condylar fracture.
    2. For a young patient with an asymmetry that was not noticed at birth, a mild form of hemifacial macrosomia is part of the differential diagnosis. Because this condition usually affects the ear as well as the mandible, the key question is whether the ear on the affected side is small or malformed. Because there is a deficiency of soft tissue and muscle, growth modification is possible only in the least affected patients with this problem.
    3. In contrast, the asymmetry after a condylar fracture is due to a restriction of growth in the condyle area caused by contraction of scar tissue created by the injury. Growth modification is possible for patients with less intensive restriction of growth. Fig 14.45
  • When a condylar fracture is diagnosed in a child, maintaining function is the key to normal growth. Function does not mean simple opening and closing hinge movements but must also include translation of the mandibular condyles.
  • Fortunately, most jaw fractures in preadolescent children can be treated with little or no surgical manipulation of the segments and little immobilization of the jaws because the bony segments are self-retentive and the healing process is rapid.
  • Treatment should involve short fixation times (usually maintained with intraoral intermaxillary elastics) and rapid return to function. Open reduction of the fracture should be avoided.
  • A functional appliance during the postinjury period (immediately before asymmetry is established) can be used to minimize any growth restriction. The appliance is a conventional activator or Bionator-type appliance that symmetrically advances the mandible to nearly an edge-to-edge incisor position.
  • Hybrid functional appliances (with buccal and lingual shields on the left and a bite block anteriorly and on the right to encourage mandibular growth and tooth eruption on the deficient left side and restrain eruption on the right) offer a way to obtain more growth on one side than the other. (after asymmetry is established).
  • Surgical intervention for a facial growth problem before adolescence has only one goal: to create an environment in which growth is possible (indicated only in patients with asymmetric deficiency in whom the abnormal growth is progressively making the problem worse, as in ankylosis).
  • The guideline: a restriction of jaw opening of less than 15 mm is unlikely to respond to growth modification, whereas an opening of 20 mm or more usually makes nonsurgical growth guidance possible.
7th-ed correction The correct term is hemifacial microsomia — the 7th edition uses "microsomia" (the line above reads "macrosomia"). Microsomia = under-development of one side of the face (the ear, mandible, and soft tissue).

II Asymmetric Mandibular Excess

(hemimandibular hyperplasia, formerly: condylar hypertrophy)

  • The most severely affected patients are candidates for early surgical intervention.
  • Growth modification to stop the excessive growth is not possible.
  • Surgical possibilities for these patients are discussed in Chapter 20.
New figure detail (7th) The hemimandibular-hypertrophy progression figure Fig 14.45 (a classic progressive deformity) now follows one patient across four ages — 8, 15, 17, and 19 years (the Age-15 panel is added), showing how a mild early asymmetry slowly becomes a major deformity if untreated.
New in 7th ed — context Comprehensive treatment after growth modification now requires "a complete fixed appliance or a series of well-designed and monitored clear aligners," reflecting the new Chapter 18 on clear-aligner treatment.
